items.title: An Isolated Group of Amazonian Hunter-Gatherers Made a Rare Request for Help From Outsiders, Raising Concerns About Forest Degradation
items.desc: Around 20 members of the Indigenous Awá tribe emerged from the rainforest and received food from neighboring villagers. The group has not made contact with the outside world in decades, so experts say deforestation may have left these individuals with no other option
items.text:
For decades, the Awá , an Indigenous tribe in the Brazilian Amazon rainforest, has lived in almost complete isolation from the modern world. That changed on November 16, when a group of around 20 men, women and children emerged from the forest’s edge.
The Awá individuals, some of whom carried spears or wore necklaces and headdresses, made contact with a government agency that supports Indigenous peoples and the Guajajara , a larger, non-isolated Indigenous group that lives adjacent to the Awá. Both reside in Brazil’s Arariboia Indigenous Territory in the northeast state of Maranhão . Guajajara members captured photos and videos of the encounter, which have been shared by the London-based Indigenous advocacy group Survival International.
The interaction lasted for several hours, Stephen Gibbs reports for the London Times , though the two groups spoke different languages, rendering communication almost impossible. Near the end, the Guajajara shared yams with the Awá, who took the offering and, smiling, retreated among the trees.
However, Guajajara spokesperson Olimpio Santos Guajajara warns this should not be taken as a heartwarming story but as a worrying sign about the sustainability of the Awá’s voluntary isolation.
“We were trying to avoid contact with them,” he tells Brazil’s Globo television network, per the London Times . Since the late 1980s, the national government has followed a no-contact policy regarding isolated tribes like the Awá, allowing the Indigenous peoples to remain away from modern society at their discretion. “Unfortunately, today they felt forced to come and make contact,” Santos says.
Sarah Shenker , head of Survival International’s Brazil office, says the pressures of illicit deforestation, cattle ranching and hunting might be pushing the tribe to its limits, forcing them to emerge from isolation to survive.
“They’ve shown so clearly for so long that they don’t want contact with outsiders,” she tells the New York Times ’ Zane Irwin. “The fact that they’ve come out now does indicate they’ve probably felt forced to. … Because their lives are so intricately related to the forest, it would be impossible to completely separate the pressures on the land.”

The Live Oak Charleston opened for bookings in April 2026, and with it, the boutique accommodation promises a balanced and restorative stay—whether you’re in the city for business or pleasure.
Located on Meeting Street in the historic district, the central location is just steps away from Charleston’s renowned dining, boutiques, and cultural landmarks. items.text:
A father-daughter entrepreneurial duo in India have pioneered a method of paper making with rhino dung harvested by locals.
Suddenly, they say, villagers who may come into conflict with rhino see them as a continual source of income, giving them a reason to protect these majestic beasts while also supporting their livelihoods.
Elrhino Stationery was co-founded by Mahesh Chandra Bora who first got the idea when he read about rhino dung paper making in Rajasthan, the scorching desert region in the west of the country.
If they could do it there, where hardly any rhino live, why not do it in Assam, home to some 2,900 greater one-horned rhinos?
The retired mining engineer got to work experimenting with production methods, knowing that the pulp to make the paper would come from the undigested plant fibers packed together in the animal’s dung balls.
The Better India writes that his first tests were done in the kitchen with his wife’s kitchen blender—no doubt endearing Chandra and the new venture to his beloved.
His daughter Nisha then left the corporate world where she had worked for 17 years to help, and in 2014 Elrhino was born.
A post shared by Elrhino Paper (@elhrinopaper)
The production process starts by trucking away rhino and elephant dung harvested by communities that live near the reserves where the animals thrive. Assam’s national parks contain some of the highest per-kilometer concentrations of rhino anywhere in the world, and protecting the animals is one of India’s great conservation success stories .

This does put some pressure on communities living around reserves like Kaziranga and Pobitora national parks. Here, where one can find between 2 and 6 Indian rhinos per kilometer, as well as elephants, the giant animals can often stray into agricultural areas, damage crops, and destroy fences.
By purchasing the animal’s dung, suddenly these affected communities see little piles of money lying all over the ground when rhino pass by, giving them a reason to turn the other cheek if they ravage a section of rice crop.
Once the dung is collected, it’s washed and boiled until the plant fibers can be recovered and then pulped. Other materials are mixed in, such as recycled paper or cotton waste, before this mixture is pressed and dried into sheets.

items.title: Survivors of Uganda's deadly landslide seek justice at the UN
items.desc: Survivors reject relocation plans they say ignore their safety, land rights and livelihoods.
items.text:
Bududa has suffered repeated deadly landslides over the years
Survivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations.
The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitution by failing to put effective disaster management measures in Bududa, a mountainous district prone to landslides.
Their case comes as heavy rains raise the risk of further landslides. They say the government relocation programme ignores their safety, land rights and livelihoods.
The UN Human Rights Committee is considering what is believed to be the first case seeking climate adaptation measures, one that could set a global precedent.
At least 33 of the 53 people who died in the 2019 landslide were children. Years later, survivors say every spell of heavy rain brings back fears of another tragedy.
William Tsama, one of the claimants, lost four members of his family.
"Victims in such situations, ignored by governments, can take them to court to compel them to help their citizens."
Uganda introduced a resettlement plan for landslide-prone areas in 2011, but progress has been limited, with relatively few people relocated.
Last month, it launched a new resettlement programme offering affected households 18m Ugandan shillings ($4,300; £3,300) to help them move to safer areas.
But some survivors have questioned whether the amount is enough to cover the cost of relocating and rebuilding their lives.
Under the programme, families can choose between receiving two acres of land, valued at 8m shillings, plus 10m shillings towards building a house, or taking the equivalent land allowance in cash, alongside the same housing grant.
The scheme is expected to benefit 1,410 households identified as living in high-risk areas.
The government has now given residents of designated high-risk areas two months, from November to December, to leave or face forced eviction.
The threat extends beyond landslides. The complainants say changing rainfall patterns and declining soil fertility have also affected farming, leaving many families struggling to secure their livelihoods.
"I want to get a new good place for my people, so even if I die, they will be okay. I am an old man, but I am doing it for my children," Tsama said.
The survivors first launched legal action in 2020 in Uganda, and received support from Ugandan environmental organisation Greenwatch three years later.

items.desc: The Office for Environmental Protection said Daera had not complied with environmental law requiring it to classify and update Special Protection Areas.
items.text:
Special Protection Areas are home to rare and threatened birds like the curlew
An investigation has found the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs is failing to protect wild birds.
The Office for Environmental Protection said Daera had not complied with environmental law requiring it to classify and update Special Protection Areas (SPAs).
Environment Minister Andrew Muir said their findings made for "uncomfortable reading".
SPAs are home to rare and threatened birds like the curlew and whooper swan, which continue to decline in Northern Ireland.
The OEP said action had not been taken to maintain or restore wild bird populations and their habitats.
The director of RSPB NI, Joanne Sherwood, said the findings were "no surprise" and called for urgent action.
A parallel investigation is looking at the same issues involving Defra and Natural England, and they have also been issued with decision notices.
In Northern Ireland, the OEP's Chief Regulatory Officer Helen Venn acknowledged that "positive steps" had been taken, but added that delays in meeting legal obligations had played a part in the significant decline of wild birds in Northern Ireland.
"SPAs are important for achieving the Executive's commitments in relation to nature, such as the strategic outcome of thriving, resilient and connected nature and wildlife in the Environmental Improvement Plan.
"This is in addition to the Executive's international commitment to protect at least 30% of land and seas for nature's recovery by 2030.
"This is why it is important for Daera to carry out its legal responsibilities in a reasonable timeframe to deliver nature recovery and in relation to the classification and adaptation of SPAs on land."
The agriculture and environment minister Andrew Muir said there was "a moral and legal obligation" to protect wild bird habitats and welcomed continuing engagement between his officials and the OEP.
"The OEP has recognised in their investigation longstanding and concerning failures to implement recommended actions to protect wild bird habitats and populations by successive administrations both in England and Northern Ireland.
"While we have a long way to go to reverse current trends, there are signs of hope and clear examples of nature recovery in action.
"However, the scale of challenge requires greater levels of support from across government to provide the necessary resources and funding to address the nature crisis."

items.title: Birds killed in blaze at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US
items.desc: Hundreds of young birds were also rescued from the fire, which comes as foie gras is under renewed scrutiny over animal welfare concerns.
items.text:
Flames engulfed Hudson Valley farm as 200 first responders arrived at the scene
A fire broke out at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US on Thursday, killing an undetermined number of birds.
The blaze engulfed several barns at Hudson Valley Farms in upstate New York before firefighters could get inside. No information has been provided as to what caused the fire.
Crews managed to rescue hundreds of young birds and hatchlings, and no workers or first responders were injured, according to local news outlets.
Foie gras, made from the fattened liver of a duck or goose, has long drawn protests from animal rights groups because the birds are force-fed. Voters in both Washington DC and Denver backed bans on foie gras sales in this month's midterm elections.
Hudson Valley Farms is in a legal battle with the state of New York over its foie gras ban
Marcus Henley, manager of Hudson Valley Foie Gras in Ferndale, New York, told local news outlet Radio Catskill that the fire destroyed two buildings housing ducks and geese.
"The building isn't there anymore," Henley said, adding that he suspected an electrical malfunction may have started the blaze, although this has not been confirmed.
The company does not disclose how many birds it hosts at one time. Commercial poultry farms can typically house thousands of birds.
Westchester News 12 reported that the emergency response to the fire in the early hours of Thursday morning involved 37 fire departments and 200 first responders.
The fire spread rapidly, and the metal-clad, wood-frame structure of the building made it difficult for firefighters to stop the flames from spreading inside the barn.
Hudson Valley Foie Gras and the local fire department did not respond to a request for comment.
Foie gras producers have long been criticised by animal rights groups due to the production process, which involves the force feeding of birds through plastic tubes, which allows them to gain over a third of their body weight in a short period of time.
New York moved to ban the product in 2019, and Hudson Valley farms have been in litigation with the state since.
At a city council hearing in 2019, Henley argued against the ban, saying that journalists who visited the farm found "nothing inhumane" about their practices.
Animal rights activist group PETA told the BBC that they will erect a billboard nearby in memory of the birds who perished, and encouraged Hudson Valley farms to donate surviving birds to local sanctuaries.

items.text:
Experts call trial results of medication that slowed cognitive decline by almost a third ‘very promising’
A pill that mimics Viagra by relaxing blood vessels and increasing blood flow to the brain can slow cognitive decline in people with Alzheimer’s disease by almost a third, a global study suggests.
Alzheimer’s is the most common form of dementia, a condition that is forecast to affect 153 million people worldwide by 2050. There is currently no cure.
In a stage three trial spanning 13 countries, including the UK, researchers found the tablet AR1001 slowed decline by 31% in patients with early Alzheimer’s disease not receiving any other treatment.
Experts not involved with the study urged caution but said the results were “exciting” and “very promising” and could signal the arrival of a “totally new treatment” for Alzheimer’s.
The findings were presented at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference in Boston.
AR1001 is a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor and from the same family of medicines as Viagra, which is used to treat erectile dysfunction.
The South Korean company AriBio, which makes AR1001, said the drug slowed decline in 604 people taking no other drugs for Alzheimer’s. In a wider group of patients taking other drugs, the tablet did not achieve statistically significant results.
Prof Tara Spires-Jones, a professor of neurodegeneration at the University of Edinburgh and a fellow at the Academy of Medical Sciences, said the results looked “very promising”.
“This drug acts through boosting blood flow and likely also directly stimulating pathways in brain cells that promote learning and memory,” she said.
Dr Sheona Scales, director of research at Alzheimer’s Research UK, said the findings were “very encouraging”, and marked “an important milestone in the search for new Alzheimer’s treatments”.
AR1001 was “especially interesting” because it was an oral drug that took a “different approach” to existing treatments, she said. “Rather than targeting amyloid, it acts on a specific enzyme and influences several other processes involved in brain function.
“The trial demonstrated a statistically significant slowing of clinical decline in participants who were not taking other commonly used Alzheimer’s medications alongside the trial drug. However, this benefit was not significant across the overall trial group.

items.title: The North Atlantic Right Whale Population Has Shrunk, Raising Concerns About the Future of the Critically Endangered Species
items.desc: The massive marine mammals are dying from ship strikes, fishing gear entanglements and other causes, which is affecting the species' ability to grow its numbers. The animals were hunted to the brink of extinction around 100 years ago
items.text:
The North Atlantic right whale population shrank slightly in 2025, raising concerns about the future of the critically endangered species.
Scientists counted 382 individuals last year, according to new numbers released this week by the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium. That’s a 1.8 percent decrease from the 2024 estimate of 389 whales.
Meanwhile, the number of reproductive females held steady at 73, according to the consortium, which is made up of scientists from the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center for Ocean Life and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
North Atlantic right whales are massive marine mammals that can weigh as much as 140,000 pounds. They spend their winters in the shallow waters off North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia and Florida, where they give birth and raise their calves. Then, they swim more than 1,000 miles north to spend the spring, summer and fall feeding in the food-rich waters off New England and Canada.
They’re one of three species of right whales, along with the North Pacific right whale and the Southern right whale . All three species are what’s known as filter feeders, meaning they use their baleen —flexible, comb-like plates that hang from their upper jaws—to tiny creatures called copepods from the water.
Commercial whalers hunted right whales to the brink of extinction by the late 19th and early 20th centuries, dubbing them the “right” whales to go after because they were relatively easy to kill and retrieve.
All three species have been protected under the U.S. Endangered Species Act since 1970. Still, the colossal creatures have been slow to recover—and their populations remain small today. Right whales can die or suffer life-threatening injuries after being struck by boats or becoming tangled in fishing gear.
“Imagine if you were wrapped in rope that moved as you moved … literally sawing into your body,” Philip Hamilton , a biologist with the New England Aquarium, tells CBC News ’ Leila Beaudoin. “It is really painful. They don’t have arms. The pain is … kind of unimaginable.”
Climate change, noise pollution and oil and gas development also threaten the whales. Rising ocean temperatures are particularly dangerous for the massive animals. As the North Atlantic heats up, copepods are moving toward cooler waters, prompting the whales to follow them into areas where they’re not protected from ship strikes and entanglements.

items.text:
Pierre before cataract surgery at Chimp Haven.
The world’s largest chimpanzee sanctuary, Chimp Haven in Louisiana, has performed its first successful cataract removal operation on one of its residents.
Pierre the chimp has long been the alpha of his social group. So when keepers noticed him withdrawing, they knew he was having trouble with his eyesight, eventually going completely blind. Originally from a research laboratory in New York, Pierre had built a reputation as a friendly and inviting presence within his social group who was quick to welcome any newcomers and help them settle into the troop.
But as his cataracts progressed, his daily routines changed. Instead of spending time with the other chimpanzees, Pierre began keeping to himself. He stopped moving around as much and increasingly relied on his hands to feel his way through his surroundings. His caregivers initially suspected he was struggling with his vision, and over the next year he became completely blind.
Over that year, Chimp Haven's care team worked closely with Dr. Kenneth Pierce, a veterinary ophthalmologist, to determine whether Pierre was a suitable candidate for cataract surgery. Pierre passed every test with flying colors and was cleared for the procedure. The operation went well, and he proved to be an excellent patient throughout both surgery and recovery.
But the surgery was only one step in the healing process. Since regaining his eyesight, Pierre returned to climbing and moving around comfortably. He can once again recognize his caregivers and navigate his surroundings without relying on touch to guide him. After spending roughly a year unable to see, he also needed to reconnect with the chimpanzees in his social group.
Reintroduction went smoothly, and Pierre's troop was excited to see him back to his normal self. His caregivers have even noticed behaviors they had not seen from him in quite some time. He no longer carries the weight of being the group’s alpha male, giving him a chance to enjoy life without the demands of leading his troop. Pierre will continue to live his best life with his troopmates and caregivers to watch over him.

items.title: For Almost 600 Years, This Enigmatic Jan van Eyck Painting Has Entranced Viewers. Could It Actually Be a Self-Portrait in Disguise?
items.desc: The new theory about the "Arnolfini Portrait" comes as London's National Gallery brings together all 10 of the artist's known portraits for the first time ever
items.text:
Christian Thorsberg | Daily Correspondent
Ahead of a new exhibition celebrating the portraiture of famed Netherlandish painter Jan van Eyck , a new theory has emerged about one of the artist’s most famous—and deeply puzzling—canvases.
At first glance, the scene in van Eyck’s 1434 Arnolfini Portrait seems straightforward: A man, dressed in black, and woman, clad in green, stand at the center of a lavish room where every detail—furniture, a dog, jewelry, oranges—is placed as though to purposefully highlight their wealth. But a closer look at the space’s geometry offers more uncanny observations. There is no fireplace, as would have been expected, and the ceiling is too low to realistically accommodate the chandelier that nonetheless dangles above their heads. Meanwhile, a convex mirror on the far back wall reveals that the pair are not alone; two figures are entering the room. The man in black lifts his hand, apparently in silent greeting, while a large inscription beside his head reads, in Latin: “Jan van Eyck was here 1434.”
Of all the details in the piece, which borders on the surreal, the identity of the man has been speculated upon the most. The leading theory derives from the 16th century, when inventory records labeling the painting as “hernoul le fin” were interpreted to be the French spelling of “Arnoul fin,” or “Arnolfini,” the surname of a wealthy Italian merchant clan who lived and worked in Bruges, Belgium, where van Eyck kept his studio.
For centuries, many art historians have supported this understanding, considering the piece to be a portrait of some members of that family. Some scholars identify the man as Giovanni di Arrigo Arnolfini, while others think it depicts his cousin, Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini. But now, as London’s National Gallery prepares to open “ Van Eyck: The Portraits ,” an exhibition, a new theory put forth about the canvas potentially turns its meaning on its head.
Writing in the exhibition catalogue , Stephan Kemperdick , a curator at the Berlin Gemäldegalerie , posits that the painting is actually a self-portrait of van Eyck and his wife. His evidence is multi-faceted. items.title: How Did Ancient Egypt's Sacred Cats Live? More Than 100 Unwrapped Mummies Reveal Poor Living Conditions, Infections and Violence Before Death
items.desc: Osteological and chemical tests on 131 museum specimens reveal that domestic cats and wild-caught jungle cats later destined for mummification suffered high rates of disease and physical trauma
items.text:
Across ancient Egypt, millions of cats were once mummified and laid to rest in sprawling animal necropolises to honor the gods. Now, a closer look at more than a hundred preserved skulls reveals that these sacred animals endured surprisingly brutal lives.
Researchers analyzed 131 well-preserved cat skulls housed at the Natural History Museum in Vienna that originally came from Beni Hassan , an ancient animal funerary site in Egypt’s Nile Valley, some 155 miles south of Cairo. The majority of skulls belonged to adult cats, mostly domestic and some wild. They were largely dated between 380 B.C.E. and 40 B.C.E Osteological and chemical examinations revealed widespread signs of gum disease, infections, healed wounds and fatal skull fractures, according to a study recently published in the Journal of Archaeological Science .
“What struck us most was the high proportion of injuries and evidence of disease, suggesting that these cats lived in poor conditions,” Bea De Cupere , study co-author and archaeozoologist at the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences, tells Phys.org ’s Sandee Oster. “This is not what one would expect for animals destined to become votive mummies.”
In ancient Egypt, cats were revered as earthly embodiments of the goddess Bastet and frequently appeared on tomb walls and artifacts. Eventually, devotees began mummifying felines as sacred offerings across at least 20 animal cemeteries in Egypt, according to the study.
In the 19th and early 20th centuries C.E., however, excavators were mostly interested in human mummies and used ancient animal remains as ship ballast, fuel, fertilizer or powdered medicine. The Beni Hassan skulls—the largest known museum collection of ancient Egyptian cat skulls with documented origin—survived only because British biologist William A. Herdman salvaged a small portion of roughly 200,000 animal mummies set out for a fertilizer auction in Liverpool in 1890, according to Gizmodo ’s Gayoung Lee. Since 19th-century scientists were mainly interested in skulls, the cats’ torsos were likely discarded after unwrapping.
To reconstruct the cats’ lives, lead author Wim Van Neer , also an archaeozoologist at the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences, and his team conducted X-ray and chemical isotope analyses alongside radiocarbon dating on nine of the skulls. 101 years ago today, Robert F. Kennedy was born. The US Senator from New York became Attorney General during his brother John Kennedy’s years in the White House—and would eventually launch his own race for president after JFK’s assassination. READ more… (1925)
Many of the civil rights initiatives championed by the Kennedy Administration and its successor were spearheaded by RFK, who was also known as “Bobby” .
On the night that Martin Luther King Jr. was shot and killed, Robert F Kennedy delivered the news to the people of Indianapolis, Indiana. Local police warned him that a riot could break out there in the heart of an African-American ghetto. He wrote his notes on the ride over and started his speech without any drafts, delivering it on the back of a Flatbed truck. Although all major US cities experienced riots, Indianapolis remained calm, thanks to RFK’s speech.
63 days after that night, RFK was assassinated at age 42 while campaigning for the Presidency. Since his death in 1968, his wife Ethel raised their 11 children and never remarried. She oversaw the Robert F. Kennedy Center for Justice & Human Rights until her death last year.
75 years ago today, Snowdonia National Park was created by British Parliament as the third national park in the country after the Lake and the Peak districts. It protects a mountainous region in northern Wales of the same name of 827 square miles of myth-shrouded mountains and valleys. Much of the park is undeveloped, but there are also many agricultural activities that go on.
The English name for the area derives from Snowdon, which is the highest mountain in Wales at 3,560 feet (1,090 meters). In Welsh, the area is named Eryri. A commonly held belief is that the name is derived from eryr (“eagle”), and thus means “the abode/land of eagles.”
Snowdonia is one of the wettest parts of the UK, and a part of Snowdonia is the wettest part. Nevertheless it remains well-visited by domestic tourists—3.5 million of whom come to partake in the serious hiking and mountain climbing on offer in the park.
For conservation purposes, the whole of the park is not totally protected as Americans would understand that phrase, but it does enjoy a particularly high number of special conservation designations—over a dozen nationally and internationally. (1951)

items.title: Medieval Readers Saw Floods, Plagues and Comets as Omens of Doom—So They Created a Mysterious Manuscript of Apocalyptic Artworks to Peruse at Will
items.desc: "The Book of Miracles," a 16th-century manuscript likely created in Augsburg, is heading to auction. It features 167 paintings of extreme weather events and strange celestial phenomena
items.text:
Ellen Wexler | Writer and Special Projects Editor
In the Bible, God’s will often emerges through natural phenomena. The great flood cleanses the earth of human corruption, while the rainbow symbolizes the divine covenant “between God and every living creature.” For millennia, worshippers familiar with these stories have wondered: What meaning can be found in the movements of storms, seas and stars?
That’s the central question of The Book of Miracles , an illustrated manuscript dating to the mid-16th century. Featuring 167 imaginative paintings, the text begins with episodes from the Old Testament and ends with apocalyptic visions from the Book of Revelation . Between them is a catalog of earthquakes , comet sightings , locust plagues , volcanic eruptions and other events spanning antiquity through the manuscript’s creation.
Now, The Book of Miracles is heading to the auction block, where it’s expected to fetch between roughly $920,000 and $1.3 million. Bidders can vie for the volume during Christie’s Valuable Books and Manuscripts sale on December 10.
“The artists of The Book of Miracles have reinterpreted historical and contemporary sources with apocalyptic panache,” per the lot listing . Illustrations of earthquakes, floods and other natural disasters that occurred in Europe are “among the most energetic, imaginative and colorful illustrations in the manuscript.”

Neighbors and total strangers rallied around an 87-year-old woman with Parkinson’s Disease named Carole, raising more than $109,000 and proving she was much less alone than she thought. All it took was one person to take the time to check on the person who lived upstairs.
Carole had lived alone for years, with no family nearby, and was struggling through her day-to-day life without much if any assistance. On top of the tremors and mobility issues caused by her Parkinson’s disease, Carole was living very near the poverty line, surviving on Social Security, SNAP, and Medicaid benefits in an upstairs apartment in Culver City, Los Angeles.
That’s when Carole got a new downstairs neighbor. Heidi Widmer arrived in Culver City from Buffalo looking for a fresh start. She was initially disappointed and frustrated to find she had a noisy upstairs neighbor—a thumping sound that she said sounded like someone bowling carried on for weeks. “I was miserable because I barely got any sleep,” Widmer recalled.
Everything changed when Carole’s tremors caused her to spill the recycling she was trying to take out right outside Widmer’s door. It had taken Carole about 20 minutes just to get down the stairs with a walker. When Widmer came out and helped her clean up, Carole’s first words were, “Thank you so much. Are you my new neighbor? Widmer realized her “loud neighbor” was really just someone trying to stay independent. “That was just such a humbling moment for me,” she said. “I’m like, no, baby girl, you’re not loud at all.”
Annoyance turned to compassion, and suddenly Carole was no longer alone. Widmer, who has always been a caregiver by nature, stepped in. She takes out the trash twice a week, cooks for Carole once a week (including homemade pierogies), and helps with cleaning. items.title: What are heat pumps and how much do they cost?
items.desc: The government wants more homes to have heat pumps to cut fossil fuel use and drive down energy bills.
items.text:
Switching to heat pumps is seen as a key way to help meet the UK's net zero targets
Developers will have to install heat pumps and solar panels in all new homes in England under regulations announced in March .
The changes are estimated to add £10,000 to the price of new homes, though owners will likely save money on energy bills over the long term.
In January, the government introduced a £15bn Warm Homes Plan to help UK households pay for green technologies as part of efforts to reduce fossil fuel use and energy bills.
But the autumn budget cut £1bn from the programme to pay for defence.
Heating homes accounts for about a fifth of the UK's planet-warming emissions, so switching from gas and oil to heat pumps is seen as a key way to help meet net zero targets .
Heat pumps run on electricity instead of gas and are more efficient than traditional boilers. They warm buildings by absorbing and amplifying heat from the air, ground or water.
Air source heat pumps - the most common type - suck in outdoor air and pass it over tubes containing refrigerant fluids. The heat from the outdoor air causes the refrigerants to evaporate into a gas. Compressing the gas increases the temperature, and this heat is passed around the home.
The system consists of a box measuring about 1m x 1m x 0.4m (3ft x 3ft x 1.3ft) which stands outside the property, as well as a heat pump unit and hot water cylinder inside the property.
The indoor unit is about the size of a gas boiler, while the size of the cylinder depends on the property.
Ground source heat pumps are more efficient than air source models.
However, they are typically more expensive and less commonly used, as they require either a deep bore hole or a large horizontal system dug into the ground.
The Boiler Upgrade Scheme provides a grant of £7,500 towards the cost of an air source or ground source heat pump for homeowners in England and Wales.
Households typically spend an additional £5,000 on top of the grant, which the UK's spending watchdog warned is too high for many .
The grant can be used for existing homes and non-domestic buildings. The property must have an eligible Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) - a measure of how your property is performing - issued in the last 10 years.
Properties no longer need to have existing loft or cavity wall insulation to qualify for the grant, which can save around £2,500 in upfront costs.

From a waterfall of fog to almighty storms and sunrises, the winners of the 2026 Weather Photographer of the Year competition have been announced.
The competition run by the Royal Meteorological Society in the UK attracted over 5,500 entrants from around the world, with the judges’ winners selected by an international panel of experts in weather, climate, and photography.
In addition, the public voted for their favorite via the Royal Meteorological Society website .
Francisco Bailón Rodríguez took 1st place with an image taken on Mallorca.
Photographed at dawn, looking towards the Formentor Peninsula, the image shows fog spilling over cliffs towards the sea. Humid nights and persistent high pressure helped the fog develop, while a southwesterly wind carried the low cloud across the rugged landscape. At first glance it becomes difficult to discern where the fog ends and the sea begins.
Runner-up was awarded to Weilu Chen, from China with a spectacular photograph of the Sun’s golden light over the Hong Kong–Zhuhai–Macao Bridge, with crepuscular rays fanning across the sky above the Pearl River Delta.
These striking beams appear as sunlight streams through gaps in the clouds, alternating with bands of shadow.
Third place was given to Laura Hedien, from the United States. Captured during a night-time storm chase, Hedien’s photograph freezes a lightning strike illuminating a supercell and the lake below.
The flash reveals a shelf cloud along the storm’s leading edge, formed as cool outflow lifts warmer, moist air ahead of it.
“A huge congratulations to all our winners and runners-up. The standard of the photographs submitted this year was incredibly high. These breathtaking images showcase the weather and climate in its pure beauty, complexity, and intensity,” said Professor Liz Bentley, Chief Executive of the Royal Meteorological Society.
In parallel to the judges’ decisions were the results of the public vote, which produced a different slate of winners led by Mahmudul Hasan, from Malaysia, with a breathtaking image of the tea-growing region of Long Coc in Vietnam.
At first light, layers of mist revealed the rounded hills in a wave-like pattern, creating a tranquil scene shaped by both weather and agriculture.
Public choice runner-up was awarded to Dan Martland, who captured a triple lightning strike over the skyline of New York City with the Statue of Liberty in the foreground.

Voyager 1, depicted in this artist’s concept, reached one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo: NASA/JPL-Caltech)
NASA’s Voyager 1 has made history. After nearly 50 years of travel, the spacecraft has reached one light-day from Earth. Launched Sept. 5, 1977, Voyager 1 is humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, traveling through interstellar space at about 38,000 mph. Voyager 1 achieved the milestone on Nov. 18 at 5:16 a.m. EST.
Light-days, like light-years, measure distance, not time. To make sense of the vastness of space, scientists measure the amount of time it takes light to travel. According to NASA, light travels at about 186,000 miles per second in a vacuum. For comparison, sunlight passing Earth reaches the moon in 1.3 seconds. As such, a light-day measures the distance light travels in 24 hours, which is roughly 16.1 billion miles.
Mission engineers confirmed the light-day milestone using trajectory calculations and the probe’s carrier signal, which conveys data to Earth. Since Voyager’s radio signal travels at the speed of light, the astronomers in charge of the probe at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory heard from the probe 24 hours after achieving this feat.
Voyager 1, and its twin, Voyager 2, launched in 1977, are the only probes built by humankind to ever go beyond our solar system. In 2012, Voyager became the first spacecraft to reach interstellar space after leaving the heliosphere , the bubble of particles and magnetic fields created by the sun that deflects cosmic radiation.
In addition to scientific instruments, Voyager 1 carries a Golden Record. Like a message in a bottle in an expansive ocean, the golden disc includes images and sounds from Earth, as well as inscriptions that show our planet’s location to any advanced civilization that may come across it.
“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” says Dave Gallagher, JPL director. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”

items.text:
Huge strides were made for the Land Back movement on Cape Cod. On October 30, 2026, approximately 126 acres of ancestral land were returned to Indigenous ownership. Given the history of the land itself, the transfer was a particularly meaningful one, more than 400 years in the making.
The land, which overlooks what is now known as First Encounter Beach in Eastham, Massachusetts, is near where the Nauset, who are part of the Wampanoag Nation, first came across a group of Pilgrims who had arrived aboard the Mayflower in 1620. While the name of the beach commemorates this historic encounter, it was also the site of a confrontation in which the Nauset defended their homeland.
The property had been in the care of The Nature Conservancy since 1986 and was recently gifted to the Native Land Conservancy, an Indigenous-led nonprofit organization based in Mashpee, a historic town located on the Upper Cape. Founded in 2012, the organization works to preserve natural landscapes while reconnecting Indigenous communities with their ancestral lands.
“This location holds so many stories that were buried and are ready to be unearthed,” said Ramona Peters, founder and board president of the Native Land Conservancy and a member of the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe.
Earlier this year, the organization also purchased a neighboring 20.4-acre property, meaning that approximately 146 acres of land in the area are now under Indigenous care. The conservation area has been given the name T8nupâhs Uwatuhshât, which translates to “at the turtle’s nest” in Wôpanâak. The name is particularly fitting, as diamondback terrapins return to the area each year to lay their eggs.
Aside from its historical and cultural significance, the land is also home to a variety of wildlife, including the diamondback terrapin and eastern box turtle. The Native Land Conservancy will continue to protect the area’s natural habitats while providing Indigenous communities with an opportunity to reconnect with the land and its history.

Johan Rockström, one of world’s leading climate experts, says slowing down scientific work puts cooperation at risk
Climate science is “foundational” to the Paris agreement and worldwide progress on tackling global heating, and attempts to delay new scientific reports threaten global cooperation on tackling the crisis, one of the world’s leading climate scientists has warned.
Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, must be allowed to work as quickly as possible on its next comprehensive assessment of global knowledge of the climate systems .
Some countries are holding up work on the three-part report in a row over the body’s role and representation of developing countries. One group has argued that racist assumptions underpin some of the body’s recommendations.
Rockström said the reports were fair. “The IPCC is objective, evidence-based science, and it’s the only thing that we can reliably stand on as a basis for our policymaking,” he said. “The IPCC is the summary of everything done voluntarily by scientists from the entire world, global south and global north, that collectively carries out a synthesis [of established research].”
The IPCC’s work is used to inform the annual climate “conference of the parties” (Cop) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. Its next assessment, called AR7, the seventh in a series dating back to 1988, under way, and it is hoped it will be completed in 2028. In the autumn of that year, nations will gather for Cop33, where the second “global stocktake” under the Paris agreement will be thrashed out.
This is the mechanism by which progress towards the core Paris goal, of limiting temperature rises to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels, will be judged. The stocktake is almost certain to find that current pledges to cut greenhouse gas emissions are inadequate and must be improved.
The UN has already found the world to be on track for a 2.8C temperature rise , a level previous IPCC reports have found would result in severe and, in some cases, irreversible consequences, such as the melting of ice caps and glaciers, sea level rises, coral bleaching and extreme weather.

items.title: Ancient Humans May Have Hunted Hippos With Poisoned Spear Tips on the Arabian Peninsula 125,000 Years Ago
items.desc: A new study suggests people hunted and processed game near a large, lush freshwater lake in what is now southern Saudi Arabia, challenging the assumption that humans just passed through the region
items.text:
Today, southern Saudi Arabia is a hot, dry desert, with sand dunes as far as the eye can see. But 125,000 years ago, it was home to a lush, freshwater lake that supported animals like hippopotamuses, buffalo, ostriches, camels, gazelles and oryx.
A new study, published November 12 in the journal Science , suggests that ancient humans took advantage of this rich biodiversity—and may even have created poisoned weapons to take down their prey.
Researchers conducted excavations at a Middle Paleolithic site known as Uruq Aljelibah, which means “sand dunes of a watering hole.” It’s located in the Empty Quarter, or Rub' al-Khali , a vast desert region spanning southern Saudi Arabia, as well as parts of Yemen, Oman and the United Arab Emirates. The evidence suggests the site was once home to a 131-square-mile lake that measured nearly 100 feet deep and was surrounded by palms, reeds, trees, shrubs and other plants, per a statement .
While investigating the site, archaeologists discovered more than 500 fossilized animal remains and more than 5,500 stone tools and artifacts, including stone points they think may have been dipped in poison to paralyze or kill big game.
The weapons were clustered near animal bones, which suggests the lakeshore was used for hunting and processing game. They also showed damage consistent with striking large animals, and some still had microscopic traces of animal tissue near their tips. Several also had chemical biomarkers associated with the arrow-poison tree ( Acokanthera schimperi ), a plant that contains cardiac glycosides , naturally occurring compounds that can affect heart rate.
The researchers also found hints of resin and fibers at the bases of the stone points, which suggests they were “hafted”—composite weapons made from multiple materials, rather than simple handheld tools.
“Hafting is often inferred indirectly, based on size and shape of stone tools, for instance,” study co-author Huw Groucutt , an archaeologist at the University of Malta, tells Haaretz ’s Ruth Schuster. “What we have done is find direct evidence in the form of residues showing how the tools were hafted and used, at a scale that is rarely applied in archaeology, and certainly not at sites like this, open air sites in arid regions.”
The scientists also discovered evidence of cutting, scraping and fiber processing, which suggests the people living here were exploiting plant resources for food, tools and binding materials.

items.text:
HMCS Spitfire was commissioned by colonial government to protect against Russian warships during the Crimean war
The wreck of Australia’s first locally built warship has been discovered 128 years after sinking off the coast of far north Queensland.
Marine archaeologists found the remains of Ex HMCS Spitfire on 21 August, the anniversary of its sinking in 1898.
Celeste Jordan, the principal heritage officer at Queensland’s Department of the Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation, said it was “remarkable luck”. Rediscovering lost shipwrecks would “help ensure the stories of our past are preserved, celebrated and protected for future generations”, she said.
The 19-metre wooden gunboat, designed and built in Sydney in 1855, was commissioned by the Australian colonial government to protect against Russian warships based at Vladivostok during the Crimean war and amid concern about the French military presence in New Caledonia. It was designed to carry a 32-pounder cannon, although evidence suggests the armament may never have been fitted.
The clipper later served Queensland as a pilot vessel, before it was sold for £300 into private hands as a sea cucumber fishing vessel.
A 1981 article in the Naval Historical Review described the boat as “a sturdy little vessel”. Constructed from ironbark and blackwood, and sheathed in copper, it was designed and built by the Sydney shipbuilder John Cuthbert, and launched by his wife Susan Cuthbert from Darling Harbour in 1855.
On 21 August 1898, Spitfire developed a leak and foundered on a voyage off the coast of Queensland’s Cape York peninsula, according to the Australian National Maritime Museum. Its crew were rescued by the Japanese steamship Omi Maru.
A crew from the Australian National Maritime Museum, the Queensland government and the Royal Australian Navy found the wreck while aboard HMAS Diamantina, a minehunter vessel. The month-long expedition searched an area based on archival records, with sonar picking up the Spitfire as an acoustic anomaly.
The chief of navy, Vice Admiral Matthew Buckley, said the Spitfire occupied a unique place in Australia’s naval history. “For sailors today, this vessel represents the beginning of a story that continues in the Royal Australian Navy.”
The wreck is protected under the Underwater Cultural Heritage Act, and is one of more than 8,000 shipwrecks, sunken aircraft and other heritage sites in Australian waters.

Some of these posts are genuinely clever, others are wonderfully silly, and a few might catch you completely off guard.
items.text:
Picture the stereotype first. A sunset in blinding colors, a cartoon coffee mug, a caption in a font that is far too large, and a cheerful instruction at the bottom to share if you agree. Anyone under thirty could describe this image from memory, which tells you boomer humor has built a very recognizable look. The funny part is that the look is only the wrapper. Underneath sits a surprisingly consistent set of comedy habits, and some of them work better than the internet likes to admit.
Start with where it lives. Harbinger Magazine’s breakdown of generational humor calls Facebook perhaps the largest home of the memes and jokes that capture boomer comedic taste.
Once plenty of Gen Z, Millennial and Gen X users drifted away, the platform became the territory of a generation with far less experience of internet culture. Reddit’s Terrible Facebook Memes community now logs the strangest finds the way bird watchers log rare sightings. What makes this stuff distinct is how literal it is.
Younger meme culture loves irony stacked on irony, the kind of joke that needs a footnote and a working knowledge of last Tuesday’s trending topic. Boomer humor goes the other way. A joke about a husband and a TV remote is a joke about a husband and a TV remote, with no hidden layer and no wink. When the setup is good, the punchline lands precisely because nobody was hunting for a secret meaning.

items.title: The NIH Has Decided to Move Its Last Group of Retired Research Chimpanzees to an Animal Sanctuary Next Year
items.desc: The agency had previously determined that the animals were too old or ill for the journey. But a recent transfer involving another federally supported research facility pushed the National Institutes of Health to revisit the issue
items.text:
Roughly three dozen chimpanzees currently live at the Keeling Center for Comparative Medicine and Research in Bastrop, Texas. They used to serve as subjects in scientific studies. Next year, however, these primates—the last federally owned chimps at an American research facility—will move to a retirement home at an animal sanctuary, according to an announcement by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) on November 18.
“Completing their transfers will fulfill NIH’s commitment, announced in November 2015, to retire all NIH-owned chimpanzees to sanctuary,” says Jay Bhattacharya , director of the agency, in the statement.
The move has been a long time in the making. In 2000, the Chimpanzee Health Improvement Maintenance Protection (CHIMP) Act established a national sanctuary system for chimps no longer needed for federal biomedical research. Then, in 2015, the NIH announced it would end its funding and support of all research on the primate species. The agency committed to retire all its approximately 300 chimps and move them to Chimp Haven , a 200-acre federal sanctuary in Keithville, Louisiana.
But the plan proceeded slowly. In 2019, the NIH veterinary panel determined that the 44 federally owned chimpanzees at the Alamogordo Primate Facility in New Mexico were too old or ill to move. Many of the retirees were near the upper end of their life expectancy in captivity and had severe health problems like heart disease. Two years later, the agency decided the same for the 51 primates at the Keeling Center and the 11 at the Southwest National Primate Research Center in San Antonio, Texas.
However, in 2024, staffing changes at Alamogordo and public pressure—including a lawsuit filed by animal welfare organizations—forced the NIH to shift its plans for the remaining chimps at the facility. They finally moved to Chimp Haven last year, meaning only the Keeling Center chimps remained at an NIH facility, given that the Southwest National Primate Research Center stopped receiving funding from the agency.
Although one elderly Alamogordo chimp died on the way to the sanctuary, the transfer prompted NIH leadership to revisit the potential transfer of Keeling Center animals, Bhattacharya says in the statement. “After careful analysis and internal consultations, NIH leadership decided to proceed.”
Chimps, along with bonobos, are our closest living relatives . We share almost 99 percent of our DNA with these two species.
Animal advocacy organizations have welcomed the news.

items.title: A Roman Cup and Hundreds of Other Treasures Unearthed in This 2,000-Year-Old Tomb Reveal the Rich Exchange Network of an Ancient Asian Empire
items.desc: The Xiongnu people dominated Central Asia for some 300 years. Now, a grave discovered in Mongolia has revealed the pastoral culture’s links to the Roman Empire, Han China and the Lelang Commandery
items.text:
Meilan Solly | Senior Associate Digital Editor, History
Some 2,000 years ago, an elite individual associated with the nomadic Xiongnu Empire was buried in style in what is now northeastern Mongolia. Their tomb, measuring nearly 240 feet in length (about four-fifths the height of the Statue of Liberty), is the largest of its kind discovered in the East Asian country to date.
Despite this impressive exterior, the tomb’s interior is surprisingly small and shallow. But it was packed with treasures that shed new light on the Xiongnu people’s links to such far-flung foreign powers as the Roman Empire and the Lelang Commandery , an administrative division of China’s Han dynasty that was based in what is now Korea.
The National Museum of Korea , the Institute of Archaeology at the Mongolian Academy of Sciences and the National Museum of Mongolia recently completed a four-year excavation of the burial, which is known officially as Tomb 160 . It’s located in Duurlig Nars , a Xiongnu burial ground with some 300 graves.
Archaeologists recovered 413 artifacts from the tomb, including a glass cup believed to be of Roman origin, a gourd-shaped silver pendant that once adorned a horse’s harness, a lacquered chariot and 15 jade pieces modeled after Han funerary goods .
The pendant resembles accessories found in Lelang tombs in modern-day North Korea, but unlike those ornaments, it boasts a crystal at its center. The jade objects, meanwhile, were fashioned in irregular shapes with intricate designs carved onto their surfaces, setting them apart from the disc-shaped bi prized by the Han as symbols of heaven.

Countries around the world are considering social media bans for children, but whether this would work in practice has been hotly debated. Now researchers are seeking answers through a major scientific study led by Wellcome, which will be the first of its kind.
Ten research projects will explore topics ranging from children’s mental health to their sleep and physical activity, comparing factors before and after the social media ban for children under 16 is introduced in the UK in spring 2027.
Backed by £9.3m of funding from Wellcome and working with more than 300,000 young people across Britain, researchers hope to provide crucial answers for those working on online safety and digital policy.
“We all know there has been a quite heated debate around the social media ban here in the UK [and] also around the world, but there is very limited scientific evidence about how social media and its restrictions [are] actually affecting the mental health of young people,” said Dr Camilla Iannone, research lead at Wellcome.
Iannone said restrictions will offer a once-in-a-generation opportunity to study at scale how social media affects young people’s mental health.
“We really don’t think that this is a simple binary question of whether social media media is good or bad, or whether restrictions work or don’t work,” she said. “Instead, the teams will study whether changing young people’s digital environment leads to meaningful changes in their mental health and wellbeing.”
Australia brought in a social media ban for under-16s last year, and other countries are also taking action,including Canada , Greece , and Denmark .

“I just needed to get back to them and be like, ‘Hey, I know it seems really silly, you’re talking about your pet lizard and you’re saying God bless you, but it made a difference,'” Dave Jacobson tells GNN.
Dave’s father was HM3 Russell Jacobson, who suffered 12 gunshot wounds and shrapnel from a grenade blast. He had been brought home to an understaffed Chelsea Naval Hospital and put in a full-body cast.
Outside, protestors against the Vietnam war heaped abuse on returning servicemen, and for Russell, who Dave described as entering the war as a “pacifist” with the aim of “healing people,” there was a sense of shame, which together with his injuries, began to seep into his very soul.

On November 14, SpaceX successfully caught the separated upper section of its massive Starship rocket as it returned from Earth orbit, marking a historic step toward the development of reusable rockets.
“That was the missing link,” SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during a livestream of the landing, reports Mike Wall at Space.com . “That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes.”
The 407-foot rocket launched for its 15th test flight from the company’s Starbase site in southern Texas on November 13. The lower stage, called the Super Heavy booster, separated during the ascent after providing the thrust needed for takeoff. The upper stage, called the Starship spacecraft, went on to complete a roughly 22.5-hour journey, which involved 14 laps around Earth and the deployment of 26 Starlink satellites.
After that, the spacecraft navigated back to Starbase, where a giant pair of robotic, chopstick-like arms captured it.
“Can you believe it?” Huot said during the livestream, reports Marcia Dunn for the Associated Press . “Look at her! Baby, she’s back!”

The historic catch brings SpaceX closer to its goal of building a fully reusable rocket. The company wants to build a rocket system that can travel to space and back with minimal refurbishments needed between launches.

This week the Empire State Building was illuminated in gold to celebrate NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft passing one light-day away from Earth.
It now takes the farthest man-made object from Earth 24 hours to send a signal back to NASA headquarters.
“The color gold is emblematic of the gold-plated copper phonograph record that is flying on Voyager,” NASA wrote on Tuesday. “The record contains sounds and images selected to portray the diversity of life and culture on Earth.”
The 12-inch gold-plated copper disc is intended as a message from humanity to any civilization that may encounter it. It includes 115 images, natural sounds, music from different cultures and eras, and spoken greetings in 55 languages.
Voyager 1 was launched in 1977 to study Jupiter and Saturn. It crossed into interstellar space in 2012 and continues to send data back to Earth nearly 50 years after its launch.
On Wednesday, the spacecraft passed one light-day from Earth: the distance light travels in 24 hours, or about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers).
NASA will be celebrating the milestone today because of the very fact that it will take one day to receive the signal sent on Wednesday.
For its part, Voyager seems to have decided to celebrate by relaying that it has a problem: something it has been wont to do of late; though considering its age and the distance it has traveled, it can hardly be surprising.
It was on Tuesday that the Voyager 1 mission team became aware that the spacecraft had stopped sending science and engineering data, though ground-based antennae were able to find its carrier signal.
The presence of a carrier signal means that Voyager 1’s Attitude and Articulation Control computer is doing its job to keep the spacecraft pointed at Earth and that its antenna, as well as its broadcast equipment, still work. The lack of data suggests the issue is with the onboard computer responsible for collecting the data from the spacecraft’s various subsystems, including science instruments, and putting it into the right format to be transmitted to Earth.

In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.
The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.
Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at $83 each, it said on Wednesday.
At that price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $19.3bn (£14.7bn) each.
So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?
In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.
He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.
Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track , and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.
Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.
Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.
But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.
Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".
Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.

items.desc: In a short clinical trial, participants who used the experimental toothbrush reported less plaque, gum inflammation and bleeding than those who used traditional nylon-bristled brushes. However, more research is required to assess the tool's safety and efficacy
items.text:
Researchers in China have reinvented a familiar tool: the toothbrush.
Brushing your teeth is an important part of your oral care routine. Both regular and electric toothbrushes rely on physically scrubbing away bacteria that can cause cavities and gum disease. But a new design, described November 4 in the journal Science Advances , features bristles that generate bacteria-killing electricity when they bend, perhaps providing a long-awaited update to the hygiene tool.
“Toothbrushes have undergone no substantive improvements beyond their mechanical function for about 1118 years to date,” the researchers write in the study. “Conventional toothbrushes often fail to establish an antibacterial environment on the tooth surface, allowing bacteria to recover and recolonize. Here, we developed an innovative self-charged toothbrush that integrates daily tooth brushing with piezoelectric functionality.”
Piezoelectric materials generate electricity when put under mechanical stress, like being squeezed or compressed. In the new study, researchers applied this property to the toothbrush by creating bristles from polyvinylidene fluoride, a material that produces an electrical charge when it bends.
The electricity doesn’t directly zap oral bacteria, however. Instead, the charge creates highly unstable molecules called reactive oxygen species in the saliva. These molecules disrupt the membranes of bacteria in dental plaque —a sticky layer of the harmful organisms, along with food particles and spit.

The largest fleet of electric school buses in New York State is up and running in a South Bronx neighborhood where childhood asthma rates are more than twice the national average.
Family-owned school bus company GVC has served schoolchildren with special needs in the Bronx for more than 30 years, and the company worked over the summer to install 23 dual‑port chargers to power 45 new electric school buses.
The buses will collectively prevent the emission of 1 million pounds of emissions per school year. Exhaust pollutants like carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and fine particulate matter pose serious threats to residents’ long-term pulmonary health, including through elevated asthma risk, and those most at risk are passengers waiting for buses and sitting on buses—the schoolchildren included.
GVC’s bus depot is located on Zerega Avenue, along a 2-mile corridor where around 2,000 school buses and 3,000 medium and heavy-duty vehicles pass every day.
“The children we transport are especially vulnerable to air and noise pollution,” Michael Townsend, Compliance Officer at GVC, said in a statement.
“Transitioning our fleet to electric is making a difference in people’s lives. The children we transport, and all those who live and work in the area, are enjoying cleaner air and quieter streets.”
Con Edison, one of New York’s largest utilities, worked with GVC from the earliest stages of their bus fleet transition, upgrading the grid to handle the demand from the bus chargers, offering a $450,000 incentive , and identifying other avenues of support from the city and state governments that could accelerate the transition.
This included the New York School Bus Incentive Program (NYSBIP) funded by the Clean Water, Clean Air, and Green Jobs Environmental Bond Act. The NYSBIP helped fund 20 of GVC’s electric buses and the 23 dual-port chargers.

“Con Edison is proud to invest in energy solutions that anticipate customers’ needs, reduce emissions, protect public health, and support New York’s clean energy transition,” said Vicki Kuo, Senior Vice President of Customer Energy Solutions, in a statement.

Inquest-style inquiry concludes iron age remains are of 15- to 22-year-old female who may have been ritually sacrificed
A coroner’s investigation into Northern Ireland ’s most venerable cold case has concluded that the victim was decapitated more than 2,000 years ago.
The inquest-style inquiry determined that Ballymacombs More Woman – the name given to iron age remains found in a County Derry bog three years ago – was between 15 and 22 years old when she was beheaded from behind with a bladed weapon.
The inquiry, hosted at the Ulster Museum on Monday, was not a formal inquest but adopted the structure and methodology of a coroner’s investigation and drew on the latest archaeological, forensic and scientific evidence to examine the death.
“The purpose of the exercise is not to impose modern legal conclusions upon the distant past, but to provide a framework through which the available evidence could be assessed and the story of a previously unknown young woman could be told,” said the coroner for Northern Ireland , Joe McCrisken, who chaired the investigation.
“Although separated from us by more than 20 centuries, she was once a living member of her community, and the investigation sought to restore, insofar as possible, an understanding of her life, death and place in history.”
The precise circumstances surrounding the woman’s death remain unknown, but evidence suggests it was part of a tradition of ritualised killing and sacrifice documented among other iron age bodies discovered across north-western Europe.
“What we have learned from this detailed research has allowed us to share her story with clarity and confidence,” said Hannah Crowdy, the head of curatorial at National Museums NI. “She has provided a significant insight into the iron age, and how we as a society have evolved over time.”

items.text:
Homo erectus was thought to have disappeared from mainland Asia roughly 400,000 years ago. But newly discovered fossils suggest that the species survived there for much longer, possibly living in southern China as recently as 184,000 years ago. The fossils also show for the first time that H. erectus was capable of living in a tropical rainforest environment.
The findings, described in two new papers published in the journal Nature , are based on recent analyses of H. erectus teeth. One paper finds that H. erectus persisted on mainland Asia for up to 216,000 years longer than previously thought, while the other indicates that the species was even more ecologically flexible than scientists assumed.
Scientists think H. erectus arose in Africa about 1.89 million years ago. It’s believed to be the first hominin species to have spread beyond the continent, with populations reaching what is now Georgia, on the border between Europe and Asia, by about 1.8 million years ago. The species continued spreading east into what is now China, eventually reaching the Indonesian island of Java.
Eugène Dubois , a Dutch anatomist and geologist, made the first discovery of an H. erectus fossil, in the early 1890s. He unearthed a skullcap and femur belonging to the so-called Java Man on the eponymous island.
H. erectus had a more modern, humanlike body than earlier hominins, with long legs and short arms suited to walking and running over long distances. The species made increasingly sophisticated stone tools, probably used fire , and hunted and butchered big game .
Scientists were excavating two limestone caves, located about nine miles apart in China’s Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region , when they stumbled upon nine hominin teeth. They used computed tomography (CT) scanning and physical examinations to investigate the teeth, ultimately determining that eight belonged to H. erectus . The identity of the ninth tooth, however, remains unknown.
Researchers also recovered ancient protein from five of the teeth, including the mystery tooth. In the four H. erectus teeth, they found a version of a protein called ameloblastin that had only previously been seen in older Asian H. erectus fossils.

items.desc: The 1.7 million gigabytes of data include more than 900 million galaxies, more than 60 million potential quasars and about 15,000 candidates of an elusive cosmic phenomenon that can help scientists understand dark matter and dark energy
items.text:
After roughly 13 months of scientific observations, the Euclid space telescope—built by the European Space Agency (ESA)—has released its first big batch of data. The observations cover an area of the sky roughly equal to 9,500 full moons as viewed from Earth, and that’s just a tiny portion of what the observatory will capture as it builds the largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos.
The contents of the 1.7-million-gigabyte data drop, unveiled on November 12, are astounding. They include more than 900 million galaxies; more than 60 million potential quasars , the bright cores of faraway galaxies; and about 15,000 candidates of an elusive phenomenon called strong gravitational lensing , which can help shed light on a cosmic mystery: the dark universe.
Euclid launched in July 2023 to journey to a spot nearly one million miles from Earth called Lagrange Point 2 , joining NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope. ESA’s instrument aims to investigate two mysterious, invisible things : dark matter, which acts as cosmic glue, and dark energy, thought to be behind the universe’s accelerating expansion. Scientists suspect that together, they make up 95 percent of the universe , but neither can be measured directly. That’s why scientists are excited about the thousands of strong gravitational lensing candidates in this batch of data.
Did you know? Another Lagrange Point 2 buddy
NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is currently en route to the second Lagrange point, where it will search for exoplanets and help unravel the mysteries of dark matter and dark energy.
Gravitational lensing occurs when light from a distant galaxy gets distorted by a galaxy between it and the light detector—in this case, Euclid. The way the light gets warped around the obstacle allows researchers to indirectly investigate the dark universe.

items.text:
Warren Buffett marked another Thanksgiving by converting thousands of Berkshire Hathaway shares into a charitable donation valued at about $5.5 billion.
In a short annual Thanksgiving message released with the donation, the billionaire investor and businessman wrote that the most powerful returns in life aren’t measured in stock prices. “Last Thanksgiving I wrote that kindness is costless but also priceless. A year later, I would only add that it compounds, and at a better rate.”
He converted 6,150 Class A shares into 9,225,000 Class B shares which were distributed to four Buffett family-led foundations. The gift continues his plan to give away essentially all of his shares of Berkshire Hathaway – the company he ran for more than 60 years.
Buffett directed the shares to the Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation , a major funder of reproductive health and Nebraska scholarships; the Nebraska-focused Sherwood Foundation , which supports education, human services, and community development in his home state; the Howard G. Buffett Foundation , which works on global food security, conflict mitigation, and anti-trafficking efforts; and the NoVo Foundation , which emphasizes gender equity, regenerative agriculture, and community resilience.
The roughly $5.5 billion Thanksgiving gift is substantially larger than the approximately $1.3 billion in shares he gave the same foundations last year, consistent with his goal of increasing the size of annual grants over time. He has said he intends to complete the transfer of his remaining Berkshire shares to the four foundations by the end of 2034. ⁠
Buffett also took a moment to thank those who helped him along the way to becoming one of the world’s richest men. “Much of my good fortune has come in the form of people who were kind to me and expected nothing in return. I’m grateful to every one of them,” Buffett wrote.
He left readers with a simple message for the season: Pay it forward.
“This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life. Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else.”

items.text:
Cooking content can be extremely popular on social media, but watching Toronto-area Chef Maddy Goldberg narrate her made-from-scratch recipes, it suddenly all tastes a little sweeter.
That’s because every Tuesday for years, Goldberg has been donating her time to prepare banquets for 100 people in need out of what she finds at the local food bank.
“POV cooking lunch for 100 people using the random food I find at the food bank,” reads a caption at the bottom of every video.
Far from just making spaghetti and meat sauce, or canned this with a side of canned that, Goldberg uses an arsenal of different techniques and flavors to make restaurant-quality dishes, like a lentil fritter spiced with caramelized onion, cinnamon, and curry powder.
Despite attending university for social work, it was the constant cooking for herself and her friends, coupled with an enthusiasm for the cooking competitions Chopped and Top Chef that baked a love of the culinary arts that saw her change her academic path.
Finding herself in the world of fine dining, she told TODAY , there were career characteristics that often disturbed her.
A post shared by Maddy Goldberg (@maddygoldberg)
“The main rule was, ‘Never run out of anything.’ The worst thing you could do was have to tell your chef you’re out of an ingredient, so you can’t complete a dish,” she says. “ So, we would just throw out so much food, it was insane.”
“I always wanted to volunteer at a food bank to understand the other side of the food system. What happens if instead of wasting the food, we gave it to a charity? How does that work?”
Goldberg would eventually leave the restaurant world in favor of private cheffing so as to make sure she had time and room to volunteer, which she began to do at Fort York Food Bank in Toronto.
A post shared by Maddy Goldberg (@maddygoldberg)
She told TODAY that anyone inspired by her work to help those in need don’t have to cook for 100 people. Go to your local food bank, she suggests, and ask what they need. You might find you already have it in your house somewhere—some jar of spice or a pile of food storage bags you’ve never used.
She now boasts 180,000 followers of her work on Instagram, where her food bank banquet prep videos go back to January of 2025, regularly make their mouths—and their hearts—drool.

If you're a photography lover and you own an iPhone, you probably have some thoughts on the way the camera processes images. So does Rian Johnson , director of the Knives Out franchise and Star Wars: The Last Jedi . This inspired him to team up with cinematographer Steve Yedlin to build an app that captures RAW image data and bypasses Apple’s regular photo processing.
“So I recently badgered my cinematographer Steve Yedlin into making my ideal iPhone still camera app,” Johnson wrote on X (formerly Twitter). “It shoots RAW, bypasses the iPhone’s look processing, and instead uses the same image processing we use on our movies.”
Named Chromagraph Camera , the app has been commended for its many capabilities, making users feel like they have a film camera in their pocket. The viewfinder is only meant to help you frame the shot, instead of showing you exactly how it will look. You can see the result after the image has been processed in your gallery. Users can also adjust color, exposure, and grain later in non-destructive edits, as the app stores full-quality RAW files.
“I’ve messed with plenty of good 3rd party tools but this is an elegant one-stop-shop, it just takes beautiful shots with Steve’s special sauce processing,” Johnson gushes. “I honestly just asked Steve (and our genius color science coder friend Eric Cameron) to make it because I take a ton of pics with my phone and wanted to have it for myself, and they figured hey, let’s put it out there. Hope you enjoy!”
While the response has been overwhelmingly positive, with many showing their experiments with the Chromagraph Camera on social media, Johnson shared that the app has a few caveats. For starters, it’s stills-only, and it’s only available on iPhone. “Huge apologies to my Android friends,” the director says. “Hardware consistency across Apple devices is part of what allows us to do this with confidence. Android devices are much more varied, and there’s no way with our small team we could dial it in for every device.”
